About: B, M and H on the axis of a uniformly magnetised cylinder (a bar magnet)

About this simulation

On screen
Top: the cylinder from the side on the same z scale as the plot, with its radius a, an arrow for M, the S and N faces, and the bound surface current Kb as dots (out of the screen) along the top edge and crosses (into the screen) along the bottom. Below: the fields on the axis against z/a in units of μ0M, with the cylinder as a heavy segment on the z-axis, a dashed level at μ0M, and Bz, μ0Mz and μ0Hz as chosen. The thin vertical line is the probe.
Controls
ℓ/a stretches the cylinder from a thin disc (0.2) to a long rod (8); the radius a stays fixed. The probe slider, its number box and presets, or dragging on the picture, move the probe along the axis from −6a to 6a. The fields selector chooses which curves are drawn.
Measured
Every value comes from the on-axis field of a uniformly magnetised cylinder, M = 106 A/m, a = 1 cm. The readouts, in the sidebar, give the shape and probe position, then Bz/μ0M, Mz/M and Hz/M at the probe; exactly on an end face, Mz/M and Hz/M read the values just inside | just outside. The number box and presets under the probe slider set exact positions, such as 0.01a either side of the north face.
Three Fields Along a Bar Magnet

Fields on the axis of a bar magnetBz, μ0Mz, μ0Hz against z/a

Guided Inquiry

1 · Stretch the cylinder

Keep the fields drawn at Bz alone and the probe at z = 0, with ℓ/a at 4. Read Bz at the centre, then move the probe to the end face at z = 2a and read it there. You will then stretch the cylinder to ℓ/a = 8 and read Bz at the centre and at the new end face, z = 4a. Before you do, predict how the two values change.

2 · H at the centre

Keep ℓ/a at 8 and move the probe back to z = 0. You will switch the fields drawn to Bz, μ0Mz and μ0Hz. Before you do, predict the auxiliary field Hz at the centre of the magnet.

3 · Crossing the north face

Keep ℓ/a at 8 and all three fields drawn. You will drag the probe from z = 3.99a, just inside the north face, to z = 4.01a, just outside it. Before you do, predict what happens to the three fields as the probe crosses the face.

4 · Squash the rod into a disc

Keep all three fields drawn and put the probe back at z = 0. You will slowly move ℓ/a from 8 down to 0.2, squashing the rod into a thin disc, while watching Hz at the centre. Before you do, predict how it changes.

5 · Crossing the face of the disc

Keep ℓ/a at 0.2 and all three fields drawn. You will drag the probe from z = 0.09a, just inside the north face of the disc, to z = 0.11a, just outside it. Before you do, predict how much Hz jumps at the face.

6 · What the three fields show

The magnet's B is the field of its bound surface current Kb = M, like a solenoid: close to μ0M in the middle of a long rod, about half that at a face, and small at the centre of a thin disc. Bz is continuous at the faces.

H = B/μ0 − M. With no free current it has no curl, but it is not zero: it starts and ends on the faces, where M stops, so Hz jumps by M at each face and points against M inside. This demagnetising field is small in a long rod and nearly −M in a thin disc.

The Physics

Three Fields Along a Bar Magnet · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim models a bar magnet as a cylinder of radius a and length ℓ, magnetised uniformly along its axis. A probe moves along the axis, and the plot gives Bz, μ0Mz and μ0Hz against z/a.

What you'll learn

  • Where the field of a bar magnet comes from.
  • How the field on the axis depends on position and on length.
  • What the auxiliary field H is, and how it differs from B and M.
  • How B, M and H behave on crossing an end face.
The magnet at the opening length ℓ/a = 4, with the probe on the axis.

What's on screen

  • Grey block: the magnet. M runs along the axis, from S to N.
  • Dots and crosses: the bound surface current Kb. A dot is out of the screen, a cross into it.
  • Blue curve: Bz. The green curve is μ0Mz and the orange curve is μ0Hz, when selected.
  • Dashed line: the level μ0M. The thin vertical line is the probe.
See itLook at the opening picture. Watch for: the dots on the top edge, the crosses on the bottom edge, and the blue curve above the heavy segment that marks the magnet.

03

Surface current: the field of the bar is the field of Kb

A uniform magnetisation has no bound volume current, Jb = ∇ × M = 0, and on the flat ends M is parallel to the normal, so no current flows there. On the curved surface, with outward normal ŝ, the bound surface current is (notes 6.1, Figure 56):

This is the current of a solenoid of the same shape with nI = M, which is why the field lines of a bar magnet look like those of a solenoid. In the sim, Kb is out of the screen along the top edge and into it along the bottom. In a long cylinder, well away from its ends, B = μ0M, and the field outside is very small.

A uniformly magnetised cylinder and a solenoid of the same shape with nI = M make the same field.
Key idea. Nothing inside the bar needs to be a current: all of its field comes from Kb on the curved surface.
See itLook at the long rod. Watch for: more dots and crosses along the longer edges, and Bz/μ0M reading 0.970 at the centre.
04

Field on the axis: the centre approaches μ0M, the face stays near half

On the axis, a strip of the curved surface between z′ and z′ + dz′ is a loop carrying M dz′ in place of nI dz′. So the field is that of a finite solenoid of the same size with nI replaced by M, where z± are the distances to the two ends (notes 6.14, Figure 57):

At the centre z+ = z− = ℓ/2, and (notes 6.15)

which is below μ0M and approaches it as ℓ/a grows: 0.894 at ℓ/a = 4 and 0.970 at ℓ/a = 8. At an end face the bound current lies on one side only, so Bz is about half: 0.485 at z = 2a for ℓ/a = 4, and 0.496 at z = 4a for ℓ/a = 8.

Bz/μ0M along the axis. The heavy segment is the ℓ/a = 4 cylinder.
Key idea. A longer rod gets closer to μ0M in the middle, but its end face stays near half of μ0M.
See itRead Bz at the centre of the ℓ/a = 4 magnet. Watch for: Bz/μ0M = 0.894 with the probe at z = 0.
See itNow put the probe on the N face, z = 2a. Watch for: Bz/μ0M falling to 0.485, about half of the dashed μ0M level.
05

The auxiliary field: H has sources of its own

The auxiliary field is H = B/μ0 − M (notes 6.18). Ampère's law in matter fixes only its curl, and its divergence is not fixed by the free current (notes 6.2):

The cylinder carries no free current, so ∇ × H = 0. But M stops at the flat ends, so ∇ · M is not zero there, and H starts and ends on the faces. At the centre (notes 6.29):

This points against M. It is −0.106 M at ℓ/a = 4 and −0.030 M at ℓ/a = 8, and it goes to zero for an infinitely long cylinder. Squash the rod to ℓ/a = 0.2 and Bz at the centre falls to 0.100 μ0M, so Hz = −0.900 M.

Hz(0)/M against ℓ/a, from the formula above.
Key idea. Without free current, H does not vanish: the magnetisation ending at the faces is a source of H, as charge is for E.
See itDraw all three fields on the ℓ/a = 8 rod. Watch for: Bz/μ0M = 0.970 at the centre, and Hz/M = −0.030, a small negative number.
See itNow squash it to ℓ/a = 0.2. Watch for: Bz/μ0M = 0.100 and Hz/M = −0.900.
06

At a face: Bz continues while Hz jumps by M

The bound current lies on the curved surface, so it cannot make the component of B along the axis jump: Bz is continuous across a flat end. Mz drops from M to 0, so Hz jumps up by M:

For ℓ/a = 8, from z = 3.99a to z = 4.01a, Hz goes from −0.499 M to +0.491 M while Bz goes from 0.501 to 0.491 μ0M. For the disc, ℓ/a = 0.2, from z = 0.09a to z = 0.11a, Hz goes from −0.902 M to +0.098 M and Bz stays at 0.098 μ0M.

The three fields across the N face of the ℓ/a = 8 rod. Hz is solid inside and dashed outside.
ℓ/a z/a

Key idea. Crossing a flat face, Bz does not jump, Mz falls by M and Hz rises by M, for a rod and a disc alike.
See itWatch the probe cross the N face of the ℓ/a = 8 rod. Watch for: Mz/M dropping from 1 to 0, Hz/M climbing from about −0.5 to +0.5, and Bz/μ0M staying near 0.5.
See itPut the probe just outside the face of the disc. Watch for: Hz/M = 0.098, Bz/μ0M still 0.098, and ΔHz = M in the zoomed inset.
07

Where it matters

  • Like electrostatics. With no free current, ∇ × H = 0 and ∇ · H = −∇ · M have the form of the equations for E with no free charge, with M in place of P/ε0 (notes 6.2). Methods for a polarised body carry over.
  • What an experimenter controls. In an electromagnet the free current fixes H through Ampère's law in matter, which is why the susceptibility is defined by M = χmH (notes 6.2).
  • Far from the bar. Along the axis the field is that of a dipole whose moment is M times the volume of the cylinder (notes 6.1).
Go deeper: what the sim holds fixed

The magnetisation is uniform, fixed at M = 106 A/m, and directed along the axis, and there is no free current anywhere. The sim gives the fields on the axis only, and the radius is fixed at a = 1 cm.

Exactly on a face, Mz and Hz have two values, so the readouts show them as just inside | just outside. Bz has one.

08

Summary

In one line. A bar magnet's field is the field of the current on its surface, and B, M and H are three different fields along its axis.

Key points

  • Kb = M on the curved surface gives Bz = μ0M ℓ/√(ℓ² + 4a²) at the centre.
  • H = B/μ0 − M, so Hz at the centre is negative: −0.030 M at ℓ/a = 8, −0.900 M at 0.2.
  • At a face, Bz is continuous, Mz drops by M and Hz jumps by M.

Common mix-ups

  • "A long enough magnet has μ0M all the way to its ends." The face stays near half: 0.485 at ℓ/a = 4, 0.496 at ℓ/a = 8.
  • "No free current means H = 0." Hz = −0.030 M at the centre of the ℓ/a = 8 rod.
  • "Everything drops by μ0M at the face." Only Mz stops.

Things to try on your own

  • Set ℓ/a = 2: Bz at the centre is 0.707 μ0M and Hz is −0.293 M.
  • At ℓ/a = 4, put the probe at z = 3a, one radius outside the face: Bz = 0.137 μ0M.
